title: The Bay Talos Guarded
short: From here you look out on Souda Bay, about 15 km of deep, sheltered water tucked behind the Akrotiri peninsula. Cretan myth had a guardian for coasts like this: Talos, the bronze giant who circled the island three times a day and stoned strange ships. Today the wind did his job and sent your ship here instead of Mykonos. The Venetian fortress islet at the mouth held out until 1715, seventy years after Chania fell, and in May 1941 this was the shore of the Battle of Crete, where the war cemetery now sits. Warships still anchor across the water. Chania itself is about 7 km west, and the Agora is your first stop.
long:
In the Argonautica, written by Apollonius of Rhodes in the 3rd century BC, the Argo comes within sight of Crete and cannot land, because Talos is on watch. He is the last of the bronze race, a gift from Zeus to Europa (in other versions, forged by Hephaestus for King Minos), and he runs the island's coast three times a day, throwing rocks at anything that approaches. His one weakness is a single vein at the ankle, closed by thin skin. In the poem Medea ruins him with the evil eye and phantoms, so that he scrapes the ankle on a rock and the ichor runs out of him like molten lead. All of this is myth, and a good one to carry into a harbour, especially since two days ago in Rhodes you went looking for that island's bronze giant, the one that stood, while Crete's was the one that ran.

The wind has done his work today, and what it brought you to is worth the detour. Souda Bay runs about 15 km long and is usually counted among the largest and deepest natural harbours in the Mediterranean, with the Akrotiri peninsula as a breakwater to the north. Ships have always come here when the weather turns, and the Venetians understood its value better than anyone. They built a fortress on the small island at the bay's mouth, mostly in the 1570s (the dates aren't firm), to control the way in.

The fortress has the best siege story in the bay. When Chania surrendered on 22 August 1645, the Venetian garrison and the townspeople who chose to leave were ferried out here unharmed, and Souda held out along with Gramvousa and Spinalonga. Venice kept all three even after giving up Candia in 1669, as a foothold for the day it might retake the island. It never did, but Souda flew the Lion of St Mark until 1715, in the Ottoman-Venetian war of 1714 to 1718: 70 years after Chania fell and 46 after Candia. Under Ottoman rule the islet later served as a refuge for Cretan insurgents, so that a rock which spent seventy years as a Venetian outpost inside enemy territory ended up sheltering rebels.

The 20th century gave the bay its next layer. On 26 March 1941, Italian explosive motor boats of the Decima Flottiglia MAS slipped in at night and crippled the heavy cruiser HMS York at anchor, and she was beached and later bombed by the Luftwaffe. Two months later came the Battle of Crete, 20 May to 1 June 1941, the first largely airborne invasion in history, code-named Operation Merkur; its decisive point was Maleme airfield, west of Chania, but the bay was part of the same fight.

The Commonwealth war cemetery sits on the shore about 1.5 km north-west of the port, and its figures are sobering. It holds 1,564 burials, roughly 860 British, 446 New Zealanders, 197 Australians and a few South African, Canadian and Indian, and more than half of the Second World War graves are unidentified. If the weather lets you and your day has room for it, a quiet minute there is a fair thing to give; if not, it is enough to know it lies on the shore you are passing.

Today the bay is still a military harbour, with Hellenic Navy facilities, a US Naval Support Activity and a NATO pier sharing the water, so you may see grey hulls across the way. A campaign designer might call it a neutral port with too many factions, which is roughly what it has been for 500 years. Nearly everyone in Chania's story arrived by this water or was evacuated through it, from Minoan merchants and Venetian galleys to Ottoman fleets, Royal Navy cruisers and, today, a cruise ship with a wind problem.

The shuttle or the line 13 bus takes about 25 minutes to cover the 7 km along the shore into town, and the islet at the mouth is worth watching for on the way. You will be set down near the Agora, the big cross-shaped Market Hall, which stands on the stump of a Venetian bastion and is your first stop.

title: Groceries on the Guns
short: This is the cross-shaped Market Hall, built 1911 to 1913 and today closed for restoration (reopening is announced for December 2026, so this is an outside view). It stands on the remains of a Venetian bastion, the Piatta Forma, part of the walls designed to keep the Ottomans out, and Eleftherios Venizelos opened it on 4 December 1913, three days after Crete's union with Greece. Chania's whole history is layered here, from Minoan, Roman and Byzantine through Venetian, Ottoman, Egyptian and Cretan State to Greek. Walk north-east about 7 minutes to Splantzia, the old Muslim quarter, and a church that changed sides.
long:
The roofline is a cross, with four wings and an entrance facing each compass point, said to be modelled on the covered market of Marseille. It was begun in 1911 and opened on 4 December 1913 by Eleftherios Venizelos, then Prime Minister of Greece and a local boy from Mournies, just outside Chania. It is closed today for restoration, with reopening announced for December 2026, so you will be reading it from the street.

The market stands on the remains of the Piatta Forma, a Venetian bastion on the line of the city's eastern walls, and part of the walls and the bastion were demolished to make room for it. A stone artillery platform built to keep the Sultan's army out was thus replaced by a hall for cheese and fish, which says a good deal about what the city wanted once the fighting was over and the people had won the right to shop.

Chania has been several towns on the same ground. Under the hill north-east of here, which you reach shortly, lay Minoan Kydonia, followed by Greek and Roman Kydonia (Rome took Crete in 69 BC) and then Byzantine rule. There was an interruption: from 824 to 961 Crete was an Arab emirate, until the Byzantines under Nikephoros Phokas took it back and built a fortress on that hill against a second Arab invasion. After 1204 Crete passed to Venice, and in 1252 Venetian colonists founded La Canea on the ancient site, where they stayed until 1645.

The Venetian city needed walls, and the walls are why the market stands where it does. From the late 1530s to 1568 new fortifications went up, designed by Michele Sanmicheli, one of the great military engineers of his day, with angled bastions, ditches and clear firing lines that a dungeon master would envy. They fell anyway, in 1645, after a 56-day siege (27 June to 22 August), and you meet the siege properly at the harbour mosque later.

Ottoman rule followed, 1645 to 1898, with one odd interruption: from 1830 to 1840 Crete was held by Mehmet Ali's Egypt, a reward for helping the Sultan against the Greek revolution, before it went back to direct Ottoman rule. Revolts came in 1866 to 1869, 1878, 1889 and 1895 to 1897, and in 1898 the Great Powers helped set up the autonomous Cretan State, with Chania as its capital. The last move came on 1 December 1913, when the Greek flag went up at the Firkas fortress and Crete joined Greece, and three days later Venizelos was here cutting the ribbon. A market in this style, in this place, was a statement that Chania was now a modern Greek city with proper stalls and civic pride, and it remained the capital of Crete until 1971, when the seat moved to Heraklion.

The list of those who have held the town therefore runs from Minoans, Greeks, Romans, Arabs and Byzantines to Venetians, Ottomans, Egyptians, the Cretan State and Greece, and you will see traces of most of them in the next hour or two. It is worth naming, for each wall, dome or vault you pass today, who built it and who took it over.

Traditionally the wings were divided by trade, with butchers, fishmongers, greengrocers, and cheese and herb sellers, and 76 shops grouped around the arms. If showers start, this is a good moment to peer through the gates and move on, since the outdoor stops are better done first today.

From here walk north-east about 7 minutes through the grid of streets to Splantzia, the old Ottoman Muslim quarter, where a plane tree with a dark legend stands near a church with a minaret and a bell tower on the same building. The minaret shows over the rooftops, so aim for it.

title: A Church That Changed Sides
short: You are in Plateia 1821, Splantzia, once the heart of Chania's Muslim quarter, where the church of Agios Nikolaos was built around 1320 as a Dominican church, became the sultan's mosque (Hunkar Camii) after 1645, and was reconsecrated Orthodox in 1918. It still carries both a minaret and a bell tower. The big plane tree is tied to a hanging story that is local legend and unverified. Coffee or raki at Platanos is the classic way to spend a few minutes here, with the church's two towers in view. Then walk about 4 minutes west, uphill, to Kastelli.
long:
The church of Agios Nikolaos on the square has two towers, a tall cylindrical minaret of about 36 m and a bell tower added in the 1950s, and it is reportedly the only building in Greece with both. Together they read like a faction map in stone.

About 1320 the Dominicans of Candia built it as a Catholic monastery church, since Chania was a Venetian colony and the friars were part of its order. After the fall of the city in 1645 the Ottomans turned it into a mosque, one of three churches converted straight after the conquest, and named it the Hunkar Camii, the Sovereign's Mosque, in honour of Sultan Ibrahim, who had launched the Cretan war. The minaret comes from that period and would have stood taller, over 40 m, with its lost conical cap. In 1918 the building was reconsecrated as an Orthodox church dedicated to St Nicholas, so that three owners have left their evidence in one set of walls.

The square itself is called Splantzia, from the Venetian word for piazza, and under the Ottomans it was the heart of the Muslim quarter of Chania, with Topanas, to the west, as the Christian quarter. Many of Chania's Muslims were Cretan converts who spoke Greek, so the line between the quarters ran along religion and administration rather than language, and the population also included Orthodox Christians, a Jewish quarter, and later Egyptian and Western merchants and consuls. It was a city of several communities with a garrison on top.

A large plane tree stands in the square, and local tradition ties it to the hanging of Orthodox clergy and rebels under the Ottomans. The name most often given is Melchisedek Despotakis, bishop of Kissamos, said to have been hanged here in 1821, the first year of the Greek revolution. The story is widely repeated and fits the year, but the sources only call it local tradition, so it stays unverified and is best taken as a hook rather than a fact, a place where the authorities made examples. Anyone curious could try to find out what the records actually say.

Another tradition holds that the little church of Agioi Anargyroi nearby was the only church where Orthodox worship was allowed in Ottoman Chania, which is also unverified and sounds a little too neat to rest on.

What is firmly documented is the ending. After 1923 and the Treaty of Lausanne most Cretan Muslims left in the population exchange to Anatolia, and their houses here were taken by Orthodox refugees from Asia Minor. When a historian says the exchange emptied Splantzia, this is what is meant, which is to say that families who had lived here for generations were exchanged for others who did not know the place at all, and the quarter changed its population almost overnight.

Today the square is the best place in Chania to sit down. The tavernas under the plane tree, with Platanos as the classic, will serve you coffee or a raki, and if it rains the awnings are well used to it. From a table you can see the Catholic, Ottoman and Orthodox layers without moving your head.

Next, about 4 minutes west and uphill, is Kastelli, the low hill behind the harbour, where the streets narrow and the surface changes. There you will look through fences at something much older than any of this, the town the Minoans burned and the clay tablets the fire baked.

title: The Town Under the Hill
short: Kastelli is the low hill above the harbour, and under its streets lies Minoan Kydonia, which you can see through the fences on Kanevaro Street and at Agia Aikaterini square. A fire around 1450 BC destroyed the town and baked its clay archive hard, and the finds include the Master Impression, a sealing of a giant figure over a walled sea-town, and a Linear B tablet recording honey for Zeus and Dionysos. Byzantine and Venetian walls sit on top of it all. From here walk down about 4 minutes to the Neoria, the Venetian shipyards on the east harbour.
long:
Looking through the fence at Agia Aikaterini square and Kanevaro Street, you see a section cut through a town, with stone walls at several levels, floor plans, and a protective roof built in 2005 to 2008. This is Minoan Kydonia. People lived on Kastelli hill almost continuously for about 5,000 years, with one gap of roughly 1150 to 735 BC. The digs began as rescue work under Yannis Tzedakis in 1964 and became the Greek-Swedish excavation in 1970, and they showed that western Crete had a major Minoan centre.

A fire around 1450 BC (sources give anywhere from 1480 to 1425) swept Kydonia as part of a wave of destruction across Crete that ended the world of the great Neopalatial towns. In one kitchen archaeologists found a clay hearth with a loom beside it and a jar holding about 3 kg of charred lentils and vetch, and the same fire baked the clay tablets in the archive hard enough to survive. Kydonia produced roughly 97 to 99 Linear A tablets, the second-largest archive of that undeciphered script after Hagia Triada, found in 1973; most record crops and livestock, though the language remains unread.

The best-known find is the Master Impression, a clay sealing a few centimetres across from the second half of the 15th century BC, stamped by a gold signet ring that has never been found. The picture shows a towering long-haired male figure in a kilt, holding a staff or spear, standing over a multi-storey complex with windows, horns of consecration and gates, on a rocky shore by the sea. Scholars disagree whether he is a king, a god, or a ruler shown as divine, and some read the town as Kydonia itself, which is possible but unprovable. The town is walled, which sits awkwardly with the old idea of a peaceful, unfortified Minoan Crete, though that "Minoan peace" is contested, and so is the claim that the Minoans were ruled by women, so it pays to be sceptical of both. It is a hard image to beat: a giant looming over a harbour town while no one has the ring.

After the fire the story keeps going. Knossos came under Greek-speaking rulers writing Linear B around 1450, and the same script turns up here. Five Linear B tablets were found at Agia Aikaterini in 1989 and 1990, dated to the 13th century BC, which makes Chania one of very few places on Crete with Linear B tablets, along with Knossos and Malia. One of them, KH Gq 5, records honey, reading roughly di-we for Zeus, one amphora, and di-wo-nu-so for Dionysos, two amphorae, so that both gods are named and Dionysos gets more honey, some 800 years before classical Greek drama. Whether that proves anything about their relationship is speculation, and Dionysos also turns up at Pylos. The name Kydonia, written ku-do-ni-ja, is certainly attested on tablets from Knossos, but nothing says a tablet found here names the town.

The town lived on in memory as well. Homer's Odyssey names the Kydonians twice and has Menelaus's ships wrecked on Crete near their coast on the way home from Troy, and Strabo ranks Knossos, Gortyn and Kydonia as the three most notable cities on the island. The Greeks called the quince the Kydonian apple, which gave English the word quince, though some linguists suspect a pre-Greek word got attached to the town. The myths give the town a founder, King Kydon, whose parentage varies with the storyteller, who makes him a son of Hermes or Apollo and a daughter of Minos, or of an Arcadian, or has Minos himself do the founding. The Minotaur and the Labyrinth are at Knossos, not here.

Later powers built on top of all this. A Byzantine fortress went up here in the 10th century to hold off a second Arab invasion, and parts of its wall survive. Venice's Castello followed, a walled upper town with the Rector's palace and the Latin cathedral, while ordinary townsfolk lived outside it until the new walls of 1536 to 1568 enclosed them. Bombing in May 1941 left the open lots that made digging possible.

The fence is the view, since the objects are in the museum, your afternoon stop. From here walk down about 4 minutes to the east harbour and the Neoria, the Venetian shipyards, long stone sheds where galleys were hauled in, one of which now holds a Bronze Age ship.

title: Dragon Lairs for Galleys
short: These are the long, arched stone sheds on the harbour edge, the Venetian Neoria, shipyards where galleys were hauled in to be built and wintered. Seventeen stand on the south side, with the Moro yards to the east, and sources say 22 or 23 in all. When the Ottomans took the city in 1645 they found galleys still inside. One Moro shed now holds the Minoa, a lashed Bronze Age ship replica rowed to Piraeus in 2004. From here follow the breakwater about 10 minutes to the lighthouse, weather and spray permitting.
long:
Each arch is the open seaward end of a long vaulted hall, about 50 m long, 9 m wide and 10 m high. Arched openings in the side walls link one hall to the next, so a galley could be hauled in stern first, out of the weather and out of sight. Dragon lairs is not a bad name for them.

The Neoria were the working heart of Venetian Chania. The first two were finished in 1526, there were 16 by 1593, and the 17th completed the south range in 1599, after which five more, the Moro shipyards, went up on the east side a few years later. That gives about 22 in all, though some sources say 23, so neither number should be taken as settled. They were used to build, repair and over-winter the galleys of Venice's Cretan squadron, and in the storm season they must have been crowded with hauled-up oared warships, with carpenters, caulkers and rope-makers working in the dark. A row of 7 survives together, and one more stands further west, the Grand Arsenal, now the Centre of Mediterranean Architecture, which is free to look at and open on weekdays until about 15:00 when an exhibition is on.

On 22 August 1645, after 56 days of siege, the city surrendered, and when the Ottomans walked into the arsenal they captured 12 galleys, still sitting in their sheds in a city that had just fallen. Souda, across the bay, was still Venetian, and ships were the one thing that could still have linked the two, which makes it a fair puzzle why they had not been put to sea.

The sheds kept finding work after that, first as Ottoman and Egyptian military stores and later as 20th-century warehouses and workshops. The upper storey of the Grand Arsenal is a 19th-century addition, so the building kept going long after the fleet it served had gone.

One of the Moro sheds, at the east end of the harbour, houses the Minoa, a branch of the Maritime Museum of Crete, whose annex is open until 31 October and costs about 3 euro. The Minoa is a replica of a 16th to 15th century BC Minoan ship, about 17 m long and about 4 m wide. It was built from 2001 to 2004 with split cypress planks lashed and sewn together rather than nailed, and fitted with oars and a single square sail. The design drew on ship images such as the Akrotiri flotilla fresco and Minoan seals. It was launched in December 2003, and in 2004 it was rowed and sailed about 210 nautical miles from Chania to Piraeus for the Athens Olympics, where it met the Olympic flame, carried on the last leg by the trireme Olympias.

Seen side by side, the two ships trace a long arc of the sea. On the hill just up the street where the Master Impression was found, a Minoan town stood on a rocky shore, with ships we know only through paintings and seals. Here a modern crew has made its best guess at one, while 3,000 years later Venice's galleys filled the sheds you are standing in front of. Minoan sailors, Venetian oarsmen, Ottoman crews and Royal Navy ships in Souda all shared the one constant of the island, the sea, and the powers that held it have mostly been trying to control who sails on it.

The Minoa also offers a gentle correction to the legend of Talos, who was said to protect Crete by stoning approaching ships. The Minoa did the opposite and sailed out, with a crew who rowed to Athens, which can be read as a modern answer to the giant.

If the weather is rough, spend your time inside the Moro shed, which is dry, and give the breakwater a miss. If it is calm enough, the next stop is a walk out along the breakwater, about 10 minutes, to the lighthouse at the harbour mouth. It is a defence the city has used for centuries, and the tower is what Chania looks like to ships coming in. Skip it if the stone is wet and spray is coming over.

title: The Minaret for Ships
short: You are at the end of the breakwater, or as near as the weather lets you get, in front of the Egyptian lighthouse, with its octagonal base, 16-sided middle and round top that people have always said resemble a minaret. Venice put a light here in the late 16th century and the Ottomans let it decay; the present tower is a 19th-century rebuild, dated to about 1839 under Egyptian rule by local accounts and to 1864 by others. From here the whole waterfront lies in front of you like a map, though if spray is coming over the stones you can look from the shore instead. Next is the domed mosque, about 15 minutes back along the breakwater and round the harbour.
long:
Stand where the breakwater runs out and turn your back to the sea, or, if the stones are wet and spray is coming over, do the same from the shore end, where the view is nearly as good and nothing is worth a fall. The tower beside you is the Chania lighthouse, and the sea-wall under your feet is the line that has kept the weather off the harbour for four hundred years.

Venice built the first light here in the late 16th century, usually dated 1595 to 1601, just as the harbour and the shipyards behind you were taking their final shape, and after the Ottomans took the city in 1645 it fell into neglect. The tower you see is a rebuild, and the sources disagree about when. Local and tourism accounts credit the Egyptians, who held Crete from 1830 to 1840 under Mehmet Ali, and date it to about 1839, which is why it is called the Egyptian lighthouse; other sources say it was rebuilt in 1864. Both agree it is a 19th-century tower, and neither date is safe enough to carve in stone, any more than the height, which is about 21 metres in some sources and 26 in others.

The shape is not in dispute. An octagonal base, a 16-sided middle section and a round top, with a stone stair inside, gave people the same thought at once: it looks like a minaret. It seemed a prayer tower pointed at the sea, standing guard over a Christian harbour that had been Ottoman for nearly two centuries. Whoever built it, the outline carries a small piece of the city's whole story in one profile. It was made an official Greek lighthouse in 1915, damaged in the Second World War, listed as a monument in 1962 and refurbished in 2005 and 2006, and today it flashes red every two and a half seconds.

Looking back from here, the whole waterfront is laid out in front of you. You can see the domed mosque on the quay, the long vaults of the Neoria, Firkas at the far end of the harbour, the Venetian walls, and behind them the hill of Kastelli where you stood this morning. Every power that wanted this island needed a harbour, and you are looking at the reason they all came. Weather like today's is exactly what the sea-wall was built for, and Bronze Age sailors, Venetian galley crews and cruise ships diverted from Mykonos have all run for shelter on this coast when the north wind came up.

Looking west across the gulf on a clear day, you can pick out the long arm of the Rodopou peninsula, where the sanctuary of Diktynna, the goddess of nets, once stood. In the myth, Britomartis, a nymph of the hunt, was pursued by King Minos for nine months until, cornered on a cliff, she jumped into the sea and was caught in fishermen's nets. The grateful islanders made her a goddess, and Strabo derives the name Diktynna from diktyon, a net. Her temple at Rodopou was rebuilt under Hadrian, but the oldest finds there date only to the late 7th or 6th century BC, so it is not a proven Minoan site, and whether she had Minoan roots is plausible but unproven. A goddess who answers a drowning person with a fisherman's net is still a fitting patron for this wall, and a party heading out to sea could do worse than to claim her.

You have walked the whole length of the harbour to stand here, so leave the tip to the wind. Walk back along the breakwater, keep the water on your right as you go round the harbour front, and in about 15 minutes you reach the low grey domes of the mosque on the quay.

title: The Pirate Raid and the Pasha
short: You are facing the domed mosque on the quay, Kioutsouk Hasan, also called Yiali Tzamisi, the Seaside Mosque. Built from 1645, right after the Ottoman conquest, it is usually called the oldest surviving Ottoman building on Crete, and it carries the name of Küçük ("Little") Hasan Pasha, given as the first Ottoman commander of the city. The minaret was lost in the 20th century and the mosque opens only for exhibitions, so you may see it only from outside. The war that put it here began with a pirate raid by the Knights of Malta in 1644; the siege of Chania lasted about two months, though the larger war ran 24 years. Next is Firkas, about 5 minutes west along the harbour.
long:
The building in front of you is a squat grey mass of domes at the water's edge, with a large central dome on four great arches and a row of smaller domes over the porch. Sources count six or seven of those, so do not take anyone's number on trust. This is the Kioutsouk Hasan mosque, also called Yiali Tzamisi, the Seaside Mosque, or the Mosque of the Janissaries. It was built from 1645, in the first years after the Ottoman conquest (some sources say 1645 to 1649), and is usually called the oldest surviving Ottoman building on Crete. Tradition says an Armenian architect designed it, though that is only tradition. The minaret was demolished in the 20th century, in the 1920s or by 1939 depending on the source, and the mosque opens mostly for exhibitions, so you will probably be looking at it from the quay, although a sign on the door may say otherwise.

It works as a victory banner in stone, since the Ottomans put their first new mosque on the quay where Venetian galleys had tied up, in full view of everyone entering the harbour. The reason goes back to 1644, when the Knights of Malta, the same order you met on Rhodes after they lost it, captured an Ottoman ship carrying, among others, a member of the Sultan's harem, and then put in at Crete. Sultan Ibrahim blamed Venice, and the combination of sea-going crusaders, a captured ship and an enraged sultan, which sounds like an adventure hook, started a war.

The Ottoman fleet left Istanbul on 30 April 1645 under Silahdar Yusuf Pasha, reached Chania on 23 June, and began the siege proper on 27 June. The sources give about 50,000 men, among them 7,000 Janissaries, 14,000 sipahis cavalrymen and 3,000 sappers, carried on some 416 ships, a few of them hired Dutch and English vessels. Against them stood roughly 12,000 Venetian defenders, described as an inadequately recruited militia, behind the bastioned walls Sanmicheli had designed a century earlier. Chania held 56 days and surrendered on 22 August 1645, though some sources say 54 or 57 days, depending on how they count.

The best story of the siege happened offshore, at the islet fort of Agioi Theodoroi, which was held by Blasio Zulian with about 30 men. According to the account, when the end came he refused to hand the place over and set mines in the fort, blowing up himself, his men and the fortress. Call it Crete's Alamo if you like, though it is closer to a doomed rearguard making sure the other side got nothing.

The Venetian garrison and the townspeople who chose to leave were evacuated unharmed to the island fortress of Souda, the one you passed on the way in, while the Ottomans walked into the Venetian arsenal and found 12 galleys still sitting in their sheds. Three churches became mosques at once, and Istanbul fired its cannon for three days in celebration. A Christian relief force of Tuscan, Spanish, Papal and Maltese ships arrived too late and failed in a counterattack on 1 October. Yusuf Pasha left a garrison of 8,000 behind and by most accounts was executed in Istanbul in early 1646 after quarrelling with the Grand Vizier.

Chania was only the opening of the Cretan War, which ran from 1645 to 1669 and reached its great set piece at the siege of Candia, modern Heraklion, which lasted about 21 years and is often called one of the longest sieges in history. Francesco Morosini surrendered it in September 1669, and Venice kept only three island fortresses, Souda, Gramvousa and Spinalonga, of which Souda held out until 1715. Chania's 56 days set against Candia's 21 years mark the difference between a militia behind a wall and a whole continent's mercenaries paying for every metre.

The building had a long second life afterwards. Following the 1923 population exchange it served as a warehouse, then as the town's archaeological museum, then as a tourism office, and it now belongs to the Port Fund. Walk west along the harbour front, past the cafes, with the fortress ahead of you, and in about 5 minutes you reach Firkas.

title: The Flag Over the Barracks
short: You are at Firkas, the Venetian bastion at the west mouth of the harbour, built around 1620. Its name comes from the Turkish firka, barracks, which is what it became under the Ottomans, along with a prison. On 1 December 1913 the Greek flag went up here to mark Crete's union with Greece, after a rebellion that began in 1866. The Maritime Museum of Crete now sits at its entrance (09:00 to 17:00, 4 euros), with Bronze Age ship models, Venetian galleys and the Battle of Crete, and it is the place to go in if the sky opens. Next is Topanas and the old Jewish quarter, about 5 minutes south.
long:
You are standing at the harbour's western gate. Firkas was built around 1620 to guard the harbour mouth, next to the San Salvatore bastion at the north-west corner of the walls. Its name is Turkish, firka, meaning barracks, because that is what it became after 1645, a garrison post and a prison whose guns over the harbour belonged to the Sultan's soldiers. It was here, nearly three centuries later, that the Ottoman story on Crete formally ended.

The union with Greece was proclaimed on 1 December 1913, on the legal basis of the Treaty of London of 30 May 1913, under which the Ottoman Empire gave up its rights to Crete. On that morning the Greek flag was raised over Firkas in the formal ceremony. The sources say King Constantine and Eleftherios Venizelos attended, and the date and the place are well established. Three days later Venizelos opened the new Municipal Market, which you saw this morning, built on the stump of a Venetian bastion.

Behind that flag lie 47 years of trouble. The Great Cretan Revolt of 1866 to 1869 is remembered above all for Arkadi Monastery near Rethymno. There in November 1866 the defenders blew up their own powder store rather than surrender, the same choice Blasio Zulian had made at the islet fort in 1645, two centuries earlier. More risings followed in 1878, which produced the Halepa Pact and limited home rule, and again in 1889 and in 1895 to 1897. Each time the island's villages emptied into the hills and the monasteries, so that almost every family had someone in the mountains.

In February 1897 insurgents raised the Greek flag on Profitis Ilias, the hill on the Akrotiri peninsula that you can see across the bay, and foreign warships shelled them. The famous story says the flagpole was shot away and a fighter named Spyros Kayales held the flag up himself until the admirals stopped firing out of respect. It is best treated as legend, since the shelling is better documented than the man with the flag. The Great Powers, Britain, France, Russia and Italy, occupied the island and in 1898 set up the autonomous Cretan State with Chania as its capital. That made the town an international place full of consuls and gunboats, and Prince George of Greece landed as High Commissioner in December 1898.

Venizelos, born in 1864 at Mournies just outside Chania, led the Theriso revolt against Prince George's rule in 1905, and George resigned in 1906. By 1910 Venizelos was in Athens, and he went on to serve as Prime Minister of Greece for a long run of terms. A rifle-carrying rebel in the hills in 1905 was head of the Greek government five years later, a rise that a campaign designer would hesitate to give a rogue. He died in Paris in 1936 and is buried on Akrotiri, on the hill of Profitis Ilias, looking down on the city. Chania stayed the capital of Crete until 1971, when the title passed to Heraklion.

The Maritime Museum of Crete is here too, and worth entering, or at least approaching, if the weather turns. It was founded in 1973 and is open 09:00 to 17:00, 4 euros, with three permanent exhibitions on the marine environment, the Battle of Crete in 1941, and ancient and traditional shipbuilding, so expect Bronze Age ship models, Venetian galleys and the 1941 gallery. It also closes the museum's long run along the harbour, since the Minoa, the ship you looked at this morning, now sits in one of the Moro shipyards at the far end, so you have seen both ends of the collection.

Walk about 5 minutes south from Firkas, away from the water and into Topanas, which the Venetians knew as the nobles' quarter and which later became the Christian quarter. Just beyond it, in the streets around Kondylaki, was the Jewish quarter, Evraiki, and the next stop is a quiet one.

title: Etz Hayyim
short: You are in the lane outside Etz Hayyim synagogue, on Parodos Kondylaki, in what was Evraiki, the Jewish quarter of Chania; it is open today until 15:00 and costs 4 euros, with a short tour from the staff. It was built as a church in the Venetian period and became a synagogue in the 17th century. On 29 May 1944 the Germans arrested the Jews of Chania, and on 9 June the ship carrying them, the Tanais, was sunk by a British submarine that did not know who was aboard. The synagogue was restored and reopened in 1999, and visitors are asked to photograph only the building. Lunch is two minutes away, and then a taxi east.
long:
The lane you are standing in is Parodos Kondylaki, in the part of Chania that was known as Evraiki, the Jewish quarter, and the building in front of you is Etz Hayyim. It is open today until 15:00, the entrance is 4 euros and includes a short tour by the staff, and photographs are of the building only, since it is a quiet place and deserves to be treated as one.

The building was a church in the Venetian period and became a synagogue in the 17th century, after the Ottoman conquest. Jews had lived on Crete for a very long time, and the community that worshipped here was Romaniote, with roots on the island going back to antiquity, neighbours for centuries of Christians and Muslims in the streets around the synagogue.

That life together ended in 1944, when on 29 May the Germans rounded up the Jews of Chania, about 250 to 275 people, though another account gives 276 arrested on 20 May, so the date and the figure are not settled. They were taken by truck to Heraklion and put aboard the steamer Tanais, along with Greek hostages, resistance prisoners and Italian prisoners of war. The Tanais had already been sunk once, by the Luftwaffe in Souda Bay on 26 May 1941, and then raised and repaired.

On 9 June 1944, about 14 nautical miles north-west of the islet of Dia, the British submarine HMS Vivid fired four torpedoes from 2,400 yards, and two hit, sinking the ship in about 12 seconds. The crew of the Vivid did not know who was aboard. Estimates of the dead run from 425 to 1,000, and sources do not agree on the figure; about 265 were Cretan Jews, and the rest were up to 400 Greek prisoners and between 100 and 300 Italian prisoners. The sinking ended the Jewish community of Crete, and Chania remembers the victims every June, with a memorial in the city.

The synagogue itself survived as a ruin, and in the late 1990s it was restored under the leadership of Nikos Stavroulakis and reopened in 1999. In January 2010 it was attacked twice by arsonists, on 5 and 16 January, and the second fire destroyed about 2,500 rare books and manuscripts, after which the congregation repaired it again. Today it is run by a mostly non-Jewish congregation that follows Sephardic customs and has written its own Haggadah, and Queen Sofia of Spain and the former King Constantine II visited unannounced in March 2006. The building has been kept alive by people who are not descended from the families whose names are remembered on its wall.

Inside you will find a courtyard and a garden, and a plaque with the names of the deported. Take the staff tour if one is starting, since it is short and the people who give it know the building better than anything written here, and the names on the plaque need no commentary.

When you come out, take your time before lunch at Tamam, on Zambeliou Street in an old hammam, about two minutes away; it is indoors and serves Cretan and Ottoman cooking, which suits a day of showers. After lunch, take a taxi east to the Archaeological Museum at Chalepa, since it is about 25 minutes on foot, which is too much in this weather.

title: Tablets, Honey and a Ring
short: You are at the Archaeological Museum of Chania at Skra 15 in Chalepa (08:00 to 20:00, 15 euros with audio guide), the end of the day. Among the finds are the Linear A and Linear B tablets from Kastelli and the Master Impression, a clay lump a few centimetres across that shows a giant over a walled sea-town, made by a ring that has never been found. Chalepa itself was the consuls' quarter of the Cretan State. When you are done, the easiest way back to the ship before 18:00 is a taxi to Souda, and with the weather bad and the roads busy you should allow plenty of time.
long:
This is the last stop. The museum opened here, at Skra 15 in Chalepa, on 16 April 2022, and the old museum in the Venetian church of San Francesco on Chalidon Street no longer holds the collection, so do not send anyone there. The new building is by Theophanis Bobotis and partners, about 6,000 square metres and triangular, emerging from the hillside and pointing towards the sea, with more than 4,100 objects on show. It is open from 08:00 to 20:00 until the end of October, closed on Tuesdays, and the ticket is 15 euros with an audio guide; the last entry is 20 minutes before closing, and the floor plan at the desk shows which room holds what.

Chalepa is worth a thought as well, as the elegant district of the Cretan State, the quarter of the consuls and of Prince George, where Venizelos's house is.

Among the small things, the Master Impression comes first, if it is on show. It is a clay sealing from Kastelli, dated to the second half of the 15th century BC and only a few centimetres across, stamped by a gold signet ring that has never been found. It shows a tall figure with long hair, a kilt and a staff or spear, standing over a multi-storey complex of windowed buildings with horns of consecration, on a rocky shore, behind walls with gates. Scholars argue about whether he is a ruler, a god, or a ruler shown as divine, and whether the town is Kydonia itself, and nobody can prove it. Somewhere in Chania, or in a looter's pocket, lies the master seal of a Bronze Age sea-town, which makes the missing ring the best quest hook in the building.

The tablets come next. Kastelli produced roughly 97 to 99 Linear A tablets, the second largest archive of Minoan writing after Hagia Triada, mostly records of crops and livestock. They survive because the fire of about 1450 BC baked them hard, so that the destruction that ended one world preserved its account books. Nobody can read the words, though the numbers and some commodity signs can be read, so we can count the sheep but not say their names. Later, from the 13th century BC, five Linear B tablets from the same dig are written in an early form of Greek. One of them, KH Gq 5, records honey offerings, roughly to the sanctuary of Zeus, one amphora of honey to Zeus and two to Dionysos. The reading is not certain, and not every tablet may be on display. Dionysos appears at Pylos as well, so Chania is not the only Bronze Age wine god. What can be said with confidence is that two gods who later appear together on the Greek stage are already on a bookkeeping tablet, and the younger one gets the bigger share.

Look also for the painted clay coffins, called larnakes, from the cemetery of Armeni, which date from about 1400 to 1200 BC and include one with a hunting scene. Armeni is near Rethymno, not Chania, so they are on loan to the story rather than part of the town. There is also the Kydonia pottery, inscribed stirrup jars that clay analysis traces to west Crete (others turned up at Thebes), and the clay bar stamped with twelve impressions from ten seals. After them comes the later Greek and Roman city, the town Strabo ranked with Knossos and Gortyn.

The day began in a bay where, in the myth, a bronze giant ran the island's perimeter three times a day to keep ships off. It has taken you over the layers of Chania, Minoan, Greek, Roman, Byzantine, Venetian, Ottoman and Greek again, with the sea as the thread through all of them. Under the hill where you stood this morning, a Minoan town counted its honey for gods whose names we can still read, and the rest of the story is who held the harbour next.

To get home, take a taxi from here to Souda. With thunderstorms forecast and the ship leaving at 18:00, give yourselves a margin and be back well before the time, since ships have always run for shelter in Souda Bay when the weather said so, and today you did too.
